title: PEREZ AND ZERAH WERE BORN FROM ONE OF GENESIS’ MOST SCANDALOUS SEXUAL ENCOUNTERS—THEN PEREZ ENTERED JESUS’ GENEALOGY
paragraphs: PEREZ AND ZERAH WERE BORN FROM ONE OF GENESIS’ MOST SCANDALOUS SEXUAL ENCOUNTERS—THEN PEREZ ENTERED JESUS’ GENEALOGY

There is a woman disguised beside a road. A grieving widower carrying his own failures. A sexual encounter neither of them will ever forget. A pregnancy. A public accusation. A death sentence. A scarlet thread tied around a tiny wrist. And generations later, one of the children conceived in that shattered story appears in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
There are chapters of the Bible we love to frame.
Genesis 38 is usually not one of them.
And if we are honest, it contains exactly the kind of family history most people would rather delete before anyone else discovered it.
Yet when Matthew opens his Gospel and begins recording the human ancestry of Jesus Christ, he does something astonishing.
He does not hide this family.
“Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar...” (Matthew 1:3).
Not buried underneath generations of respectable names.
Right there on the opening page of the New Testament.
And once you understand what happened in Genesis 38, those few words in Matthew can stop you cold.
Because Perez did not come from a neat story.
the story kept moving toward Jesus.
That does not mean God approved of everything that happened.
Grace never requires us to rename sin as righteousness.
It means something far more beautiful:
human sin and human wreckage were not powerful enough to derail the redemptive purpose of God.
Maybe that is why this story feels so personal.
Because some of us have things in our history we desperately wish we could rewrite.
Something carrying consequences long after everybody stopped talking about it.
You can smile in church while still wondering whether your worst chapter has quietly disqualified you from ever becoming useful to God again.
And suddenly an ancient genealogy starts sounding like good news.

She married Judah's son Er, but Genesis says Er was wicked before the LORD and died. According to the family obligation operating in the narrative, Judah's next son, Onan, was expected to preserve his deceased brother's line through Tamar. Instead, Onan deliberately prevented the offspring from being raised for his brother. Genesis condemns his conduct, and he also died.
Tamar had now lost two husbands.
Judah then told her to remain a widow until his younger son Shelah grew up.
But Judah did not give him to Tamar.
That detail matters because Genesis itself later gives Judah's confession.
After everything exploded into the open, Judah said of Tamar:
The Hebrew is even more striking:
In context, the sense is that Tamar was more in the right than Judah concerning what had happened. Judah himself explains why: he had failed to give her his son Shelah.
This does not turn every action in Genesis 38 into a model Christians should imitate.
The man who would soon be ready to condemn Tamar had failed in his own responsibility toward her.
After his mourning, Judah traveled toward Timnah for the shearing of his sheep.
She removed her widow's clothing, covered herself with a veil, and positioned herself where Judah would pass.
He did not recognize his own daughter-in-law.
He believed her to be a prostitute and propositioned her.
Tamar asked what he would give her.
But Tamar wanted a pledge until payment arrived.
And Judah walked away without realizing that the woman with whom he had just slept was the daughter-in-law whom he had failed.
The story could almost disappear there.
Except sin and secrecy have a way of colliding with daylight.
About three months later, word reached Judah.
He demanded that she be brought out for judgment.
The same man who had participated in the act did not yet know he was condemning the woman carrying his children.
And this is where Genesis 38 becomes almost unbearably human.
Because hypocrisy is often most confident before it recognizes itself in the evidence.
Tamar did not deliver a long speech.
Then came essentially one devastating question:
And the courtroom inside his own heart collapsed.
The man pointing outward suddenly had nowhere left to point.
She is more in the right than I.
There is something here every believer needs to hear.
Repentance begins when we stop editing the evidence.
When we stop explaining why our sin was understandable.
When we stop measuring ourselves against somebody who looks worse.
When we stop asking, “What did they do?”
Judah's confession did not erase the past.
But the story did not end with his exposure.
During childbirth, one baby stretched out his hand. The midwife tied a scarlet thread around his wrist to mark him as the one who appeared to be emerging first.
The midwife tied shani—scarlet/crimson—upon his hand.
Genesis preserves the midwife's startled words:
The wording plays directly on the Hebrew root פרץ — p-r-ts, associated with breaking or bursting through.
A child breaking unexpectedly into the world from a story already fractured by death, deception, sexual sin, neglect, hypocrisy, grief, and public shame.
Then Zerah emerged with the scarlet thread still on his hand.
If Genesis 38 were merely a human scandal, perhaps we would expect the Bible to leave these people there.
Then Matthew opened the story of Jesus Christ.
Matthew could have simply written Judah and Perez.
“Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar...”
The scandal is not airbrushed out of the Messiah's genealogy.
It is remembered inside the story that leads to Him.
Do not misunderstand what this means.
Jesus did not come because sin was harmless.
Jesus came because sin is devastating.
The Gospel is not God saying, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
The cross declares exactly the opposite.
Sin is so serious that redemption required the spotless Lamb of God.
Yet grace is so astonishing that Christ willingly came into a human history filled with sinners to save sinners.
He entered our world without becoming corrupted by our sin.
He did not inherit Tamar's guilt.
He did not inherit Judah's guilt.
He did not participate in their sin.
He came to save His people from their sins.
That is the shock of Matthew 1.
Before Matthew tells us about Christ's public ministry, before the Sermon on the Mount, before the miracles, before Calvary, he gives us names.
Then the genealogy arrives at Jesus.
As though Scripture were telling every ashamed person reading:
Look where God was taking the story.
Maybe your family tree has names nobody mentions.
Maybe your childhood contained things you still cannot comfortably explain.
Maybe you were born into circumstances that made you feel unwanted.
Maybe your parents' decisions became wounds you had to carry.
Maybe the scandal has your fingerprints on it.
Maybe you promised God you would never do it again...
And somewhere along the way, shame taught you a theology Jesus never preached:
God can forgive other people, but He probably cannot do much with me now.
Your origin is not your Savior.
Your family history is not your Savior.
Your reputation is not your Savior.
Your worst decision is not your Savior.
Your ability to repair yourself is not your Savior.
And this is where cheap grace must be rejected.
Perez appearing in Christ's genealogy is not permission to continue comfortably in sin.
Grace does not say, “Stay where you are.”
The same Gospel that announces forgiveness calls us to repentance.
Bring the secret into His light.
Stop defending what Scripture calls sin.
Stop pretending the wound does not hurt.
Stop using yesterday as permission for tomorrow's rebellion.
Not when you have cleaned yourself enough.
Come because you cannot cleanse your own soul.
The blood of Jesus does what reputation management never can.
Maybe somebody reading this has spent years trying to keep the scarlet thread hidden.
The thing attached to your story.
But Christianity was never the announcement that respectable people can save themselves.
It is the announcement that a Savior has come.
People who thought their story had already reached the final sentence.
This is why the Gospel is greater than inspirational self-improvement.
Jesus does not merely help you feel better about the old person.
In Him there is forgiveness and new life.
Grace does not simply repaint ruins.
So maybe the question is no longer:
“How could God possibly use someone with my history?”
“What could Jesus write with a life completely surrendered to Him?”
Perez could not choose the circumstances of his conception.
Neither can you choose every chapter that brought you here.
But you can hear the Gospel today.

And if grace has already rewritten chapters you once thought were beyond redemption, tell somebody what Jesus has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needs to read tonight.
Do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody you know may be silently convinced that their scandal has placed them beyond the reach of Christ.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
Not because anyone should pressure you into giving. Scripture says giving should come from a heart that has decided freely, “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But supporting Gospel work can be an act of willing generosity offered for God's glory.
Invite the believer who is drifting.
Invite the person who thinks Christianity is only for people who already have their lives together.
Invite even the unbeliever who has questions.
Most of all, pray that through everything Gospel Warrior publishes, they encounter the message of Jesus Christ crucified and risen for sinners.
Because Genesis 38 does not finally leave us staring at sexual scandal.
until the genealogy arrives at Jesus.
And Jesus is where every story of redemption must ultimately lead.
Your scandal may explain part of your past.
It does not have the authority to become your god.
It does not get the final word.
But none of those truths make Jesus less powerful to forgive the repentant sinner and transform a surrendered life.
Perez was born into a story people might have wanted erased.
God did not erase his name.
Generations later, Matthew wrote it down.
And immediately beyond all those generations stands the name above every name:
So when the enemy opens the file marked scandal, remember where the Gospel takes the story.
Not into pretending sin never happened.
Because perhaps the detail you thought made your story unusable...
is the very place where, one day, people will look and marvel at what the grace of Jesus Christ has done.
The scarlet thread was visible. The scandal was real. But neither one got the final word. Jesus did.
